topics.importance_evidence: Prerequisite, not a named clause: the word 'induction' does not appear in the GATE 2027 CS syllabus, which I downloaded and read in full (CS_GATE2027_Syllabus.pdf, IIT Madras, 30 October 2026). The syllabus does name the results induction establishes - Section 1 'Combinatorics: counting, recurrence relations, generating functions' and Section 5 'Asymptotic worst case time and space complexity'. GATE General Aptitude names 'Logic: deduction and induction', which is empirical generalisation and a different thing; the lesson keeps the two apart. No GATE CSE item examining induction directly could be verified, so the lesson carries no previous-year question.

a fixed point answers 'for which q does f(q) return q'
abs() takes an int in C, so the snippet is answered as mathematics
missing base case: stack exhaustion, undefined behaviour in C
unreachable base case: f(n) = f(n-2) with base n == 1 misses even n
a test placed after the recursive call can never stop the descent
tail position: no work left after the call
the C standard does not require tail call optimisation
accumulator, loop and plain recursion agree on 1..n
static local inside a recursion is one object shared by all frames
array parameter is a pointer, so every frame writes one array
a local array inside the function is a fresh copy per frame
returning the address of an automatic local dangles
two calls in one expression have no defined evaluation order
T(n) = T(n-1) + 1 gives n+1 calls; T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n gives n log2 n + n
g(n) = 2g(n/2) makes 2n-1 calls at depth 1 + log2 n
a print on both sides of a recursive call gives 3 2 1 1 2 3
value question and cost question are two computations over one tree

member offsets, alignment and padding
sizeof of a struct and the trailing round-up
field order and its effect on size
nested structures
arrays of structures and their stride
unions, overlapping members and union size
byte reinterpretation and byte order
enumerations: values, underlying type and duplicates
self-referential structures and pointer-to-struct declarations
microtopics: a struct declaration creates a type; only an object owns bytes
offset is measured from the start of the object, not from the previous member
alignment is a divisibility constraint on the starting address, not on the value
x86-64 System V sizes and alignments: char 1, short 2, int and float 4, long, double and pointers 8
each of those types is self-aligned, so alignment equals size on this ABI
offset = ceil(running / align) * align, then running = offset + size
sizeof = ceil(end / largest align) * largest align
char, int, char is 12 with offsets 0, 4, 8 and 6 bytes of padding
int, char, char is 8 with 2 bytes of padding; the same members, a different size
all six permutations give only 8 and 12: two give 12 and four give 8
widest-alignment-first reaches the smallest size, as a heuristic and not a theorem
the trailing round-up exists so that arrays of the struct stay aligned
padding bytes have unspecified values, so memcmp on a struct compares them
a nested struct's alignment is the maximum alignment among its own members
struct Inner {char; int} is 8 bytes with alignment 4; after a char in an outer struct it sits at offset 4 and the outer is 12
the inner struct's own trailing padding is counted once, not twice
an array's stride is sizeof, so struct P {char; int} gives 80 bytes for ten elements and holds 50
element k starts at base + k * stride, aligned whenever the base is
a union's members all start at offset 0 and overlap
a union's size is its largest member rounded up to its largest alignment
union {char[5]; int} is 8, not 5
GATE CSE 2000 Q1.17: short[5] plus a union of float and long is 18 ignoring alignment, and 24 aligned
writing one union member and reading another reinterprets bytes, not values
0x12345678 as four chars is 78 56 34 12 little-endian and 12 34 56 78 big-endian
character access is always permitted (C11 6.5p7); other reinterpretation may yield a trap representation
an enum names integer constants and stores one integer
an unwritten first enumerator is 0 and each next is one more
an explicit value resets the counter; duplicates are legal
sizeof(enum) is the size of the underlying integer, not the number of enumerators
a struct may hold a pointer to its own type and not an object of its own type
struct node {int; node*} is 16 bytes with the pointer at 8 on x86-64
struct node *s[10] is an array of ten pointers (80 bytes), not ten nodes
a packed struct of the same three members is 6 bytes, so layout is an ABI fact
on a 32-bit ABI the same node is 8 bytes, because the pointer is 4

free and the lifetime of an allocated block
the four heap faults: leak, use after free, double free, lost pointer
dynamic-array growth by doubling and its amortised cost
the arithmetic of allocation: sizeof, multiplication overflow, terminators
fragmentation: total free bytes against the largest hole
microtopics: storage duration is a lifetime, not a location
text, rodata, data, bss, heap and stack as a loader convention, not a C rule
a file-scope int with an initialiser lands in data, without one in bss
static storage duration is zeroed once, before main
automatic and allocated objects start indeterminate
the stack grows down and the heap grows up, toward each other
a chunk is an 8-byte size word plus the bytes you asked for
request2size(req) = max(32, (req + 23) & ~15) on glibc x86-64
usable = chunk - 8, and usable is never less than the request
requests 1 to 24 all give one 32-byte chunk with 24 usable bytes
16-byte alignment and the 32-byte minimum chunk
the extra usable bytes are an implementation detail, not a promise
malloc returns uninitialised storage
a recycled block often still holds the previous tenant's bytes
calloc zeroes every byte, and its two arguments let the multiplication be checked
all-bits-zero is zero for integers and not promised to be 0.0 or a null pointer
malloc(0) is implementation-defined: NULL or a pointer that must not be dereferenced
malloc returns NULL on failure and the check is not optional
realloc grows in place, or moves and copies min(old, new), or fails
the new tail after growth is undefined, not zero
realloc invalidates the old pointer even when the block grew in place
realloc on failure does not free the old block, so p = realloc(p, n) leaks
realloc(NULL, n) is malloc and realloc(p, 0) is implementation-defined
free returns the chunk to a bin and writes nothing into the bytes
free cannot change your pointer, because it receives a copy
free(NULL) does nothing; free of a non-returned or already-freed pointer is undefined
a freed chunk is reused, so a stale pointer may silently name a new object
leak: the block exists and no pointer reaches it
dangling: the pointer exists and the block does not
use after free is undefined and is allowed to look like success
double free and free of an interior pointer are undefined
returning the address of a local is dead on arrival (GATE CSE 2001 Q2.18, P1)
writing through an uninitialised pointer is undefined before lifetime matters (P2)
a returned malloc block survives the return (P3)
growth by one copies n(n-1)/2 elements, which is quadratic
doubling copies the old capacities, so the total is 2^ceil(log2 n) - 1
16 appends copy 15 elements and 17 appends copy 31
total copies stay below 2n, so the average per append is constant
one append can still cost O(n): amortised is not worst case
sizeof(p) is the pointer and sizeof(*p) is the element
n * sizeof(T) is computed in size_t before malloc is called
2^30 times 4 wraps to 0 in a 32-bit size_t
the safe test is n > SIZE_MAX / sizeof *p, a division that cannot overflow
calloc(num, size) is required to return NULL when the product cannot be represented
a string of length L needs L + 1 bytes
six 32-byte chunks fill 192 bytes and three frees leave 96 free
request2size(40) is 48, so a 32-byte hole cannot serve it
the largest hole decides an allocation, not the total free
C cannot compact, because it hands out real addresses
malloc asks the kernel for pages with sbrk or mmap only when it must
that is why malloc does not always make a system call (GATE CSE 2021 Set 1)

topics.topic: Graphs as a data structure: matrix, list and incidence
subtopics: the adjacency matrix and its symmetry
the adjacency list and its entry count
the edge list and the incidence matrix
space: n^2 bits against n + 2m entries
the cost of an edge test and of neighbour enumeration
powers of A: walks, degrees and triangles
the degree sequence and what it cannot decide
microtopics: a graph is (V, E); n vertices and m edges
a simple graph has no loop and no parallel edge
A[i][j] = 1 exactly when {i, j} is an edge
an undirected edge sets two cells, a directed arc sets one
the adjacency matrix of an undirected graph is symmetric
A[i][i] = 0 for a simple graph; a loop puts 1 there, or 2 in some conventions
the entries above the diagonal number exactly m
the sum of all entries is 2m undirected and m directed
a row sum is the degree; for a digraph it is the out-degree and a column sum the in-degree
the degrees sum to 2m, so the number of odd-degree vertices is even
m is at most n(n-1)/2 for a simple undirected graph
the matrix is sized by n alone, so an empty and a complete graph cost the same
the adjacency list is n heads plus one chain per vertex
chain entries total 2m undirected and m directed
a vertex appears on exactly as many chains as its degree
an edge appears twice in an undirected list, once per endpoint: the twins
setting every twin pointer costs Theta(n + m) with a table (GATE CSE 2016 Set 2 Q41)
a nested search for the twin costs O(mn), which is O(m^2) on a dense graph
in-degrees in a list need a second set of chains or a full scan
the edge list stores m pairs and forgets adjacency entirely
the incidence matrix is n by m, one column per edge
every column of an undirected incidence matrix holds exactly two ones
incidence row sums are the degrees and the ones total 2m
incidence rank over GF(2) is n - c and the nullity is m - n + c
over the reals the unsigned incidence rank is n - c only for bipartite graphs
the nullity is the dimension of the cycle space
a packed matrix needs ceil(n^2/8) bytes; a 32-bit matrix 4n^2
a list needs 4n + 16m bytes under 4-byte heads and 8-byte nodes
at n = 1000 the list wins while m < 7,562
at n = 6 the packed matrix wins outright, so 'lists are smaller' is about density
hasEdge is O(1) on a matrix and O(deg) on a list
enumerating neighbours is Theta(n) on a matrix and Theta(deg) on a list
a whole traversal is Theta(n^2) on a matrix and Theta(n + m) on a list
the tightest bound on DFS with an adjacency matrix is Theta(n^2) (GATE CSE 2014 Set 1)
transposing a matrix is Theta(n^2); a list transpose is Theta(n + m)
A^k[i][j] counts walks of length k from i to j
the diagonal of A^2 is the degree sequence for a simple graph (GATE CSE 2022 Q10)
off the diagonal, A^2 counts common neighbours
the sum of A^2 is the sum of the squared degrees
the diagonal of A^3 is twice the triangles at that vertex
trace(A^3)/6 is the number of triangles (GATE CSE 2022 Q12)
six is three corners times two directions
A = A inverse forces every degree to 1, so the graph is a perfect matching (GATE CSE 2024 Set 2 Q7)
the matrix is defined only after the vertices are labelled; relabelling conjugates it
a degree sequence does not determine a graph
K3,3 and the triangular prism are both 3-regular on 6 vertices with 9 edges
K3,3 has no triangle and the prism has two
Theta(n^2) is linear in the input size when the graph is dense
a tree has m = n - 1, so a connected graph is always list territory

two-dimensional arrays: row-major and column-major
bounds, decay and sizeof in C
stacks and their applications
postfix evaluation and infix to postfix
reachable stack permutations
queues, circular queues, deques
implementation trade-offs
one structure built from another, and their costs
microtopics: an array is one contiguous block plus index arithmetic; nothing stores the index
address of a[i] = base + (i - L) * w, with w the size of the element type
a[i] is defined as *(a+i), so indexing is pointer arithmetic plus a dereference
random access is O(1); insert or delete in the middle is O(n) shifts
row-major: the second index varies fastest, so the multiplier is the number of columns
column-major: the first index varies fastest, so the multiplier is the number of rows
the two orders agree exactly when one dimension has length 1
GATE 1998: A[1..10][1..15], w=1, base 100, row-major gives 15i + j + 84
C does not check bounds; a[n] on T a[n] compiles and is undefined behaviour
a[-1] is undefined for the same reason: the pointer leaves the object
an array name decays to a pointer except under sizeof, unary &, and string initialisation
sizeof inside a callee measures a pointer, so the length must be passed
a stack is LIFO: one insertion end, one deletion end, the same end
on an array: top = -1, push writes a[++top], pop reads a[top--]
empty is top == -1 and full is top == N-1; capacity N holds N elements
overflow and underflow belong to the array implementation, not to the ADT
postfix places each operator after its operands, so no precedence rules are needed
the first pop is the right operand; only minus and divide expose an order error
GATE 2007: after the first * the top two are 6 and 1, not the final value 2
infix to postfix by a precedence stack, and a bracket matcher as the minimal stack use
reachability: push until the wanted element is on top, then pop; if it is buried, reject
GATE 1994: of the four orders only 3,4,5,2,1 is reachable
3, 1, 2 is impossible: it contains the pattern 312
the number of reachable orders is Catalan C(n) = (2n)!/((n+1)! n!)
a queue is FIFO: insertion at the rear, deletion at the front
a linear array queue drifts: rear reaches the end while front cells are unusable
circular queue: rear = (rear+1) mod N, and front the same
front == rear means both empty and full once every cell may be filled
sacrifice convention: empty front == rear, full (rear+1) mod N == front, capacity N-1
count convention: empty count == 0, full count == N, capacity N
count = (rear - front + N) mod N under the sacrifice convention
GATE 2012: capacity n-1 in an array of n gives the sacrifice pair, answer A
queue from two stacks: pour only when the output stack is empty
that queue is amortised O(1) because each element crosses at most once
stack from two queues: every pop is Theta(n); there is no amortisation
two stacks in one array: overflow exactly when top1 + 1 == top2, holding all N

topics.topic: Linked lists
subtopics: singly and doubly linked lists
insertion and deletion
the head pointer and pointer surgery
cost trade-offs against arrays
circular lists
reversal and merging
cycle detection
microtopics: a node holds a value and the address of the next node; a link is an address, not an index
index arithmetic is replaced by a stored address, so access becomes O(k) instead of O(1)
the list is not an object: it is the head pointer plus the chain that pointer reaches
struct node may contain struct node * because the pointer needs only the name, not the complete type
NULL terminates the list; the empty list is head == NULL and dereferencing NULL is undefined behaviour
sizeof(struct node) includes padding, so it is not the sum of the members
no length is stored: counting costs a walk, or a separate count every mutation must maintain
insert after p: x->next = p->next; p->next = x — two writes, and the order is mandatory
writing p->next = x first makes the old successor unreachable: a leak, not a compile error
GATE 1998 Q19a: q = p->next; p->next = q->next; q->next = (q->next)->next; (p->next)->next = q swaps the two nodes after p
the fourth line reads (p->next)->next, whose target has already changed by then
delete after p is one write, but the victim must be saved before it is unlinked
inserting at the front changes the head; a by-value head parameter cannot report it
three repairs: return the new head, take node **, or use a dummy header node
GATE 2010 Q36: q->next = NULL; p->next = head; head = p — detach, attach, then move
reach element k: O(1) array, O(k) list
a sorted linked list cannot be binary-searched: the middle is only reachable by a walk
insert at position k is O(n) in both, for different reasons: shifting against walking
delete the node you were given: O(n) singly, O(1) doubly — GATE 2023 Q03, GATE IT 2004
the copy-the-successor trick is O(1) for interior nodes and has no move for the last node, so the worst case stays O(n)
the trick also changes which node object survives, so other pointers to it silently see different data
doubly linked invariant: b->next->prev == b and b->prev->next == b
a doubly linked splice in the middle writes four fields; a singly linked one writes two
deleting x from a pointer to x: x->prev->next = x->next; x->next->prev = x->prev — two writes, no walk
GATE 2016 Set 2 Q15: the decrease-key term dominates, because restoring sorted order is a walk, giving O(N^2)
a circular list has no NULL; a traversal needs a supplied count or a saved starting node
GATE 2004 Q36: point the single pointer at the rear, so the front is one link away and both operations are O(1)
pointing at the front instead makes enqueue walk the whole ring
GATE 1997 Q1.4: concatenation in O(1) needs the tail without a walk — circular doubly linked, head->prev, four writes
reversal uses three cursors; next must be saved before curr->next is overwritten
reversal writes exactly n links in n steps: Theta(n) time, O(1) extra space — GATE 2022 Q05
the recursive reversal is Theta(n) time but Theta(n) space, so it does not answer an O(1)-space question
merging two sorted lists relinks existing nodes and needs at most n1 + n2 - 1 comparisons
cycle detection: tortoise one link, hare two; meeting proves a cycle, the hare reaching NULL disproves it
with the cycle entering after mu links and repeating every lambda, they meet within mu + lambda steps
the meeting node is not the entry node; a second phase with one cursor restarted at the head finds it
GATE 2017 Set 1 Q08: a valid NULL-terminated list may be empty, so join may dereference NULL
GATE 2003: f(p) returns 1 exactly when the list is non-decreasing
inserting n keys into a sorted list costs n(n-1)/2 comparisons, so the total is quadratic (GATE 2020)

topics.topic: Trees, binary search trees and heaps
subtopics: tree terminology and traversals
BST operations and properties
balanced tree ideas
binary heaps and heap operations
heapsort
microtopics: a binary tree is a shape: root, internal nodes, leaves, and an ordered left and right child
depth is per node from the root; height is per tree to the deepest leaf; the root is at depth 0
n0 = n2 + 1 for every non-empty binary tree, proved by counting edges two ways
full (0 or 2 children), complete (last level filled left to right), perfect (2^(h+1) - 1 nodes)
preorder, inorder, postorder and level order differ only in when the root is visited
preorder starts with the root; postorder ends with it; inorder of a search tree is sorted
preorder + inorder or postorder + inorder rebuild a tree; preorder + postorder does not
the two-node tree is already ambiguous for preorder + postorder: a single child has a side
the search-tree promise quantifies over whole subtrees, not over parents
the parent-only test accepts root 10, left child 5, right child of 5 equal to 12 — which is not a BST
an increasing inorder is necessary and, for a tree, sufficient; the bounds test is the direct check
a search path is a sequence of narrowing bounds: left lowers the upper bound, right raises the lower one
GATE 2008: of four sequences only III can be the path taken while searching for 273
GATE 2008: only 'II is an inorder of some BST with root 121 and 52 a leaf' is true
insertion is a failing search, so every new key becomes a leaf and costs the height
the same keys in two insertion orders give two trees; the set fixes the inorder, not the shape
sorted insertion gives a chain, so search is Theta(n) and the worst-case height is n-1
GATE 2016 Set 2: a BST with 15 nodes has height at least 3 (perfect tree) and at most 14 (chain)
GATE 2015: inserting 71, 65, 84, 69, 67, 83 puts 67 alone at the lowest level
GATE 2022 in substance: with the insertion order unknown, only the inorder is determined by the key set
the number of shapes on n nodes is the n-th Catalan number, from T(n) = sum T(k-1) T(n-k)
GATE 2003: the index that completes the Catalan sum is x = n-k
the number of BSTs on n distinct keys equals the number of shapes, because the inorder fill is unique
GATE 2008: 3 distinct keys give 5 trees; GATE 2005: 4 keys give 14; GATE 2007: 3 unlabelled nodes give 5
GATE 2011: a given unlabelled shape with n distinct keys has exactly one BST filling
n! counts insertion orders and overcounts trees, because different orders can build the same shape
deleting a leaf or a one-child node is one pointer write; two children need the inorder successor
the successor is the leftmost node of the right subtree, or the first ancestor turning right
GATE 2016 Set 1: deleting the i-th node of a heap of depth d is one repair path, O(log n)
a heap makes two promises: complete shape, and parent no larger than child
a heap does not order left against right, so it is not a search tree and its inorder is not sorted
base 0: children 2i+1, 2i+2, parent floor((i-1)/2), leaves floor(n/2) to n-1
base 1: children 2i, 2i+1, parent floor(i/2), leaves floor(n/2)+1 to n
the maximum of a min-heap is a leaf, so it has as many candidate indices as there are leaves
GATE 2024 Set 1: a 105-key min-heap indexed from 1 has 53 possible indices for the maximum
GATE 2021 Set 2: finding the maximum in a min-heap is Theta(n)
GATE 2025: a min-heap of 32 keys has height 5
GATE 2016 Set 2: the integer 9 in a heap of 1 to 1023 cannot go deeper than depth 8, since only 8 keys are smaller
insert appends at the next free slot then sifts up against the parent only, O(log n)
remove-min moves the last leaf to the root then sifts down against the smaller child, O(log n)
the last leaf is the only position whose removal keeps the shape complete
GATE 2021 Set 1: in a complete BST on 1000 nodes the 3rd largest key is at index 509
bottom-up build starts at the last internal node and sifts down back to index 0, in one pass
the build is O(n) because at most n/2^(h+1) nodes sit at height h; the level sum is at most 2n
heapsort is O(n log n), in place, not stable, and no better on nearly sorted input
the comparison table: sorted array, search tree and heap against search, insert, minimum, delete-min, in-order

topics.topic: Complexity classes: P, NP, NP-hard and NP-complete, and what a reduction proves
subtopics: the class P: decided in polynomial time
the class NP: a polynomial certificate checked by a polynomial verifier
P contained in NP, and the open question of strictness
NP-hard: every problem in NP reduces to it
NP-complete: NP-hard and in NP, two independent conditions
polynomial-time many-one reductions and their direction
3-SAT to CLIQUE, with the correspondence in both directions
CLIQUE to VERTEX COVER through the complement
the boundary cases: 2-SAT in P, fixed-size clique in P, NP-hard problems outside NP
microtopics: a decision problem answers yes or no; an optimisation problem is not one until rewritten
P is bounded by a polynomial in the input length, so n cubed qualifies and 2 to the n does not
at n = 40 a cubic method needs 64000 steps and exhaustive search needs 1099511627776
2 to the n overtakes n cubed at n = 10 and stays above it thereafter
NP is not the phrase 'not polynomial'; it means non-deterministic polynomial time
certificate length is polynomial in the input; for 3 variables there are 8 candidate certificates

certificate 100 satisfies all four clauses, one literal per clause doing the work
exactly 4 of the 8 assignments are accepted: 100, 010, 001 and 111
a decider wrapped in a verifier that ignores the certificate shows P is contained in NP
the wrapper returns the same answer for three different certificates, because it reads none
NP-hard quantifies over all of NP, so one reduction from one problem proves nothing
the halting problem is NP-hard and outside NP, since NP holds only decidable problems
NP-complete = NP-hard and in NP; NP-hard alone does not imply membership
SAT and 3-SAT are NP-complete by the Cook-Levin theorem
a reduction is a polynomial-time f with x in A exactly when f(x) is in B
hardness flows along the arrow: A NP-hard and A reduces to B makes B NP-hard
membership flows against the arrow: B in NP and A reduces to B makes A in NP
reducing a candidate to 3-SAT proves membership only, never hardness
the reduction graph puts one vertex per literal occurrence: 4 clauses give 12 vertices
two vertices are joined when they lie in different clauses and are not opposites: 42 of 66 pairs
no two vertices of one clause are adjacent, so a clique takes at most one per clause
a clique of size 4 picks one compatible literal per clause and so satisfies all four
the graph has 12 cliques of size 4 and no clique of size 5
the number of cliques need not equal the number of satisfying assignments: 12 against 4
a clique reads back to an assignment (100 here) and an assignment reads forward to a clique
the unsatisfiable 8-clause instance has a 24-vertex, 204-edge graph with largest clique 7
largest clique below the clause count is exactly the reduction answering no
the complement of a graph on n vertices has n choose 2 minus m edges: 10 minus 5 = 5 here
a clique of size k in G is a vertex cover of size n minus k in the complement
on the worked example the largest clique is 3 and the smallest complement cover is 2, and 3 + 2 = 5
the identity is checked on all 1088 graphs with four or five vertices; a check is not a proof
2-SAT is in P via the implication graph and its strongly connected components
the component test agrees with brute force on 3060 four-clause 2-CNF formulas
clique with k fixed at 3 costs n cubed, so hardness needs k in the input
NP-hard is wider than NP-complete; NP-complete is NP-hard intersected with NP
if any NP-complete problem is in P then P = NP = NP-complete, one class instead of three

the linear-time construction from a depth-first search
bridgeless against 2-vertex-connected, and closed against open ears
the boundary cases and the decision procedure
microtopics: an orientation is one direction per edge; strong means every ordered pair reaches
a bridge is an edge on no cycle, and its deletion raises the piece count
one bridge is enough to kill every strong orientation, whichever way it points
an ear is a walk with both ends in the built part and every inside vertex new
an ear may be one edge long, or closed (a cycle), or a multi-edge path
the first ear must be a cycle because nothing is built before it
every later ear has both ends in the union of the earlier ears
the construction: any cycle first, then walk unused edges until the walk comes home
no used edge touches an unbuilt station, so all its streets are unused
a station of degree one ends a bridge, so bridgeless gives every station degree at least two
the walk cannot stall, and a finite edge set forces it back to built ground
with a bridge the walk reaches the far side and stops
one ear with k edges brings k edges and k-1 stations, so the rank rises by one
number of ears = |E| - |V| + 1, fixed by the graph and not by the construction
the worked map: 11 streets, 8 stations, rank 4, four ears (4, 3, 3 and 1 street)
the bowtie: rank 2, and its second ear is closed at the shared station
K4: rank 3, and 24 of its 64 orientations are strong
a tree: rank 0, no first ear, no strong orientation
orient ear one round and every later ear end to end, and the whole graph is strong
the induction: a directed path between two stations of a strong part keeps it strong
Robbins 1939: strong orientation exists iff connected and bridgeless
the search orientation: tree edges away from the root, other edges from descendant to ancestor
the tempting variant, every edge from the earlier discovery number to the later, is acyclic and fails
bridgeless is about edges, 2-vertex-connected is about stations: the bowtie
Whitney 1932: open ear decompositions exist exactly for the 2-vertex-connected graphs
closed ears are the loophole that lets a graph with a cut station have a decomposition
boundary cases: one station (in, vacuously), two stations one street (out), parallel edges (in)
loops are never bridges and never help reachability
disconnected graphs are out even with no bridge anywhere
exhaustive checks: all 64 graphs on 4 stations, all 848 on 5 stations with at most 6 streets
the five-step procedure, and why a yes answer needs a construction and a check

topics.topic: The optimal binary search tree
subtopics: cost as a weighted sum of levels
the range-weight lemma
optimal substructure
the recurrence and its base cases
the triangular table and its fill order
reconstruction from the root table
why the greedy root rule fails
ties and non-uniqueness
the contrast with Huffman coding
complexity and counts
microtopics: level of a key = comparisons to reach it, root at level 1, not depth 0
cost(T) = sum p_i * level_i; average = cost / total weight
no tree costs less than the total weight, since every key needs one comparison
weights may be counts or probabilities; scaling scales the cost and nothing else
fixing the root splits the range into i..r-1 and r+1..j, with no interleaving
pushing a subtree down one level adds its total weight once, a weight not a count of keys
cost(T) = cost(left) + cost(right) + W(i,j), and W does not depend on the shape
optimal substructure holds precisely because W is shape-independent
C(i,j) = W(i,j) + min over r of C(i,r-1) + C(r+1,j)
base cases C(i,i) = p_i and C(i,i-1) = 0
the table is a triangle: n(n+1)/2 cells, 10 for four keys, 21 for six
fill by increasing length; cells of the same length never read each other
row-major fill happens to work at n=4 and fails at n=5
R(i,j) stores the argmin; walk it from R(1,n) to rebuild the tree
the rebuilt tree must re-add to the table entry, which is the cheap self-check
worked instance 4 2 1 3: table values 4, 2, 1, 3 / 8, 4, 5 / 11, 10 / 19
top level of that instance: 20, 19, 21, 21, so the root is key 20 and the cost is 19
greedy on the same instance gives 20: root 10, then 40, then 20
greedy on 3 3 1 1 gives 16 against the optimum 14
the greedy failure is structural: a root is paid for by every key in the range
ties: weights 5 45 45 5 give 160 with two optimal roots and two optimal trees
all the weight on one key makes a chain optimal, so shallow is not the goal
equal weights make the balanced tree optimal: three keys cost 5 of 3
Huffman: symbols at leaves, no ordering constraint, greedy merging is optimal
the search tree: keys at internal nodes, ordering constraint, greedy fails
alphabetic coding (Hu-Tucker) keeps the order but still stores symbols at leaves
Huffman on 5 45 45 5 costs 165 against the search tree's 160; the numbers measure different objects
Huffman's tree groups keys 1 and 4 with 2 and 3 apart, so no left-right choice makes it a search tree
counts: trees on n keys is Catalan(n) = 1, 2, 5, 14, 42, 132
naive time is cubic, space quadratic; Knuth's bound gives quadratic time under a monotonicity condition
the unsuccessful-search variant only adds the external weights into W

topics.topic: Magnitude comparators, code converters and the BCD adder
subtopics: magnitude comparators and cascading
code converters: binary, Gray, BCD, excess-3
the BCD adder and its correction network
microtopics: a specification maps an input word to an output word, so it is a table of 2^n rows and 4^n for two words
two eight-bit words would need 65536 rows, which is why the table method is replaced by a state
one-bit comparator: G = a AND NOT b, E = a XNOR b, L = NOT a AND b, one gate each
G + E + L = 1 in every row: mutual exclusion plus exhaustiveness, checked on all four rows
the state passed up the chain is the triple (greater, equal, less) about the higher bits
G_out = G_in OR (E_in AND a>b), L_out = L_in OR (E_in AND a<b), E_out = E_in AND (a=b)
the identity element is (0, 1, 0), the statement that the bits above the top are tied
comparison reads most significant first; the first differing bit decides and no lower bit is consulted
1011 against 1001 is decided at bit 1 and bit 0 is never consulted
the ripple agrees with numeric comparison on all pairs up to six bits, checked by enumeration
of the 4^n ordered pairs, 2^n tie and the remaining split evenly: 16, 120, 120 at four bits
swapping the two words is a bijection between the greater and the less pairs
cascading two four-bit comparators: the low stage's flags drive the high stage's tie input
a cascade input of (0, 0, 0) makes the high stage report less on every pair with differing high nibbles
equality of two n-bit words costs n XNOR plus n-1 AND, so 15 gates at eight bits
equality is an AND over the whole word, never an OR of per-bit equalities
a code is a spelling of a value; a converter changes the word and not the value
BCD uses ten of the sixteen four-bit words; 1010 to 1111 have no digit to mean
Gray(n) = n XOR (n >> 1); g_i = b_i XOR b_i+1 with b_n = 0
decoding is cumulative: b_i = g_i XOR b_i+1 with the binary bit above already decoded
binary 1011 becomes Gray 1110, and Gray 1110 decodes back to 1011
Gray is a bijection, consecutive words differ in one bit, and the wrap 15 to 0 differs in one bit
the Karnaugh map axis 00 01 11 10 is the two-bit Gray sequence, which is why one-bit-different labels touch
counting order 00 01 10 11 would place two-bit-different labels adjacent and break every group across that edge
excess-3: code(d) = binary(d + 3), self-complementing because inverting four bits computes 15 minus the value
inverting excess-3 gives the nines complement, not the tens or ones complement
no excess-3 codeword is all zeros or all ones, which is its second useful property
BCD adder: two digits plus a carry in give a true sum of 0 to 19 split as carry out and low nibble
the repair is to add six, because six is 16 - 10, so the nibble becomes s - 10 and the carry appears
the correction condition is C_out + S3 S2 + S3 S1, exact on all sixteen nibbles
S3 S2 covers 1100 to 1111 and S3 S1 covers 1010, 1011, 1110, 1111; together exactly 1010 to 1111
S3 alone is not the condition: 1000 and 1001 are valid digits with S3 = 1
9 + 9 + 1 = 19 has a valid-looking nibble 0011, so only the carry out reveals the correction
the correction always raises the carry out of the second adder
all sixteen nibbles occur across the 200 valid inputs, so 1010 to 1111 are reachable here and not don't-cares
the same six words are genuine don't-cares at a BCD-to-excess-3 converter's input, where they never arrive
verified against decimal addition on all 200 valid inputs: digit and carry both agree
the three problems share one method: name the words, find the small state, write the per-position rule, check it exhaustively

eccentricity of a vertex
diameter, radius, centre, periphery

leaf peeling for the centre of a tree

height of a breadth-first-search tree against the diameter
the square of a graph and its diameter

the distance table is symmetric with a zero diagonal, so eccentricity is a row maximum
eccentricity is a maximum, not an average; the row mean is no graph quantity here
diameter = max of the eccentricities = max over pairs of d(u,v)
radius = min of the eccentricities; centre and periphery are the two arg-sets
ceil(d/2) <= r <= d, proved from the triangle inequality with a centre vertex
the floor is attained by trees, the ceiling by cycles, complete graphs and Petersen

Euler trail and Euler circuit: definition and the parity condition
the Euler criterion in full: even degrees and one component, undirected and directed
Hierholzer's walk-and-splice, and what it costs against Fleury's rule
the cycle decomposition that proves sufficiency, and counting Euler circuits
Hamiltonian path and cycle, and why deciding them is NP-complete
Dirac's and Ore's sufficient conditions, and the counterexample that shows they are not necessary
necessary conditions that work: bipartite balance and c(G - S) <= |S|
the Petersen graph, hypohamiltonicity, and the line-graph link between the two questions
microtopics: walk, trail, path, circuit and cycle as five different objects, each rationing a different thing
an Euler circuit rations edges and may revisit vertices freely; a vertex of degree 2k is passed k times
a Hamiltonian cycle rations vertices and uses exactly n edges, ignoring every other edge
each pass through a vertex uses two of its edges, so a closed trail forces every degree even
an open trail leaves one unpaired edge at each of exactly two vertices, and those are its endpoints
the number of odd-degree vertices is always even, because the degrees sum to twice the edge count
Konigsberg: four land masses of degree 3, 3, 3, 5, four odd vertices, so no trail, confirmed by search
the Euler criterion needs both clauses: even degrees and the edge-carrying vertices in one component
two disjoint triangles are all even and have no circuit; joined at a vertex the bowtie is Eulerian
isolated vertices are ignored: the clause is about the vertices that carry edges
directed: in-degree equals out-degree everywhere, plus one component on the arcs; balance plus weak connectivity forces strong connectivity
the directed trail case: one vertex one greater out, one one greater in, everything else balanced
Hierholzer: walk until stuck, then splice a cycle at a vertex the tour already visits
the first walk on the bowtie closes in three edges, and one splice at vertex 1 completes 0-1-3-4-1-2-0
Hierholzer is O(V + E); Fleury pays for a bridge test at every step
an Eulerian graph decomposes into edge-disjoint cycles, and that decomposition is the proof of sufficiency
K(5) decomposes into 0-1-2-3-4-0 and 0-2-4-1-3-0, sharing every vertex and no edge
K(5) has 132 Euler circuits; 528 traversals from vertex 0 over 2 directions and 2 visits agrees
rotation and reversal are the same circuit, so a naive sequence count is four times too large on K(5)
deciding a Hamiltonian cycle is NP-complete (Karp 1972); a proposed cycle is verified in linear time
brute force examines (n-1)!/2 cycles: 181,440 at n = 10 and about 3.1 x 10^23 at n = 25
Dirac 1952: n >= 3 and minimum degree at least n/2 is sufficient
Ore 1960: every non-adjacent pair with degree sum at least n is sufficient, and weaker than Dirac
the six-cycle fails both and is Hamiltonian, so neither condition is necessary
a bipartite graph needs equal sides; K(2,3) has a Hamiltonian path and no cycle
c(G - S) <= |S| for every S is necessary, and checking it is NP-hard; the Petersen graph satisfies it
the Petersen graph: 10 vertices, 15 edges, degree 3, girth 5, non-Hamiltonian, and hypohamiltonian
the Petersen graph has no Euler trail either, because all ten degrees are odd
L(G) is Hamiltonian exactly when G is Eulerian, which is the structural link between the questions
GATE CSE 2007 Q23: option A fails on connectivity, option B on parity, option C holds at degree 22
the complement of C(25) is 22-regular with 275 edges and connected, so it is Eulerian
the Euler criterion agrees with brute force on all 1086 graphs with 4 or 5 vertices and 256 sampled with 6
the directed criterion agrees with brute force on all 63 digraphs on three vertices

topics.topic: Resolution refutation, clausal form and Horn clauses
subtopics: clausal form and the conversion from a formula
the resolution rule and the resolvent
soundness of the rule
refutation completeness
the empty clause and what it means
Horn clauses
unit propagation and linear-time Horn satisfiability
microtopics: a clause is a disjunction of literals, and a set of clauses is a conjunction of them
a literal is a variable or its negation; a unit clause has one literal; the empty clause has none
clausal form: drop the biconditional and the implication, push negations inwards, distribute, split
the distribution step is what turns a formula into a set of clauses, and skipping it leaves nothing to resolve
the negation of an implication is a conjunction, so negating a goal usually adds several clauses
the empty clause is falsity and the empty set of clauses is trivially true, and the two are opposites
the resolution rule: from (A or p) and (B or not p) infer (A or B), with one pivot only
the pivot must be positive in one parent and negative in the other; agreement on a variable gives nothing
the resolvent is the union minus the pivot pair, with repeated literals collapsed
a resolvent containing a variable and its negation is a tautology and is dropped
soundness by the two cases on the pivot: the pivot is true, or it is false, and no third case exists
the resolvent is entailed by its parents and is weaker than them, never equivalent
adding a resolvent preserves satisfiability in both directions, so a satisfiable set never reaches the empty clause
refutation-completeness: an unsatisfiable finite set always has a refutation (Robinson 1965)
not derivation-complete: from the single clause (P) nothing is derivable, although (P or Q) is entailed
entailment is tested by adding the negation of the goal, never by resolving the knowledge base alone
a refutation read as a tree: original clauses as leaves, two parents per step, the empty clause as the only root
the four-clause refutation in three steps, with every original clause used once
a Horn clause has at most one positive literal, which is at most one conclusion
one positive literal is a rule or a fact; zero positive literals is a goal clause
unit propagation marks the facts, then fires every rule whose premises are all marked
every mark is forced, so the marked atoms are the smallest model of a satisfiable Horn set
a violated goal clause, all of whose literals are marked, is exactly unsatisfiability for a Horn set
Dowling and Gallier 1984: Horn satisfiability in time proportional to the literal occurrences
unit propagation is complete on Horn sets and incomplete in general, demonstrated on four clauses with no unit
no conflict from propagation means no refutation was found, not that a model exists
cancelling two complementary pairs in one step is unsound: (P or Q) with (not P or not Q)
the witness for that unsoundness: P true and Q false satisfies both parents
the two legal steps on that pair give (Q or not Q) and (P or not P), both tautologies, both dropped
duplicates and subsumed clauses are dropped as well as tautologies, and the page keeps a set rather than a list
completeness is about existence, not size: the pigeonhole clauses grow 6, 73, past 900 (Haken 1985)
GATE CSE 2003: the resolution rule for (P or R) and (Q or not R), which statement is FALSE, answer (B)
option A of that item is soundness, option B is its converse, option C is satisfiability preservation
the five-step procedure and the five traps that produce a plausible-looking clause

topics.topic: First-order resolution and unification
subtopics: terms, atoms and substitutions
the unification algorithm
the most general unifier
Skolemisation and clausal form in first order
first-order resolution with unification
refutation, lifting and Herbrand
the limits: semi-decidability and equality
microtopics: a quantified sentence is not a ground clause, and instantiating it may never terminate
a term is a constant, a variable, or a function symbol applied to terms, and is drawn as a finite tree
two terms are equal exactly when the trees match node for node, names included
nesting makes the term universe infinite from finitely many symbols
a substitution is a finite map from variables to terms and never touches constants
applying a substitution reaches every occurrence at once, and substitutions are idempotent
composition means apply the first then the second, and it is associative but not commutative
{x/y} then {y/a} makes x into a, while the other order leaves x alone
the disagreement set: walk two trees in lockstep to the first place the symbols differ
a variable against any term is repairable; two different symbols are a clash; a variable inside its own value is the occurs check
the binding is applied before the walk continues, which is why f(x,x) against f(a,b) dies at the second argument
the occurs check is a correctness condition, not an optimisation: no finite term satisfies x = f(x)
the most general unifier: every other unifier is it followed by some substitution, theta = sigma . theta2
the MGU is unique up to renaming of variables, and the least specific rather than the most
matching is unification with one side fixed, so a against f(y) fails where x against a succeeds
renaming apart is required, and without it the occurs check silently refuses not P(x) with P(f(x)) or Q(x)
prenex form first, then Skolemisation one existential at a time
a Skolem symbol has one argument per universal quantifier to its left, and none gives a constant
Skolemisation preserves satisfiability and not equivalence, so the form is strictly stronger
the quantifier swap that is not allowed: for all x exists y does not give exists y for all x
first-order resolution: rename apart, unify one complementary pair, apply the MGU to everything else
factoring replaces two unifiable same-sign literals by their instance and strengthens the clause
soundness: a resolvent is entailed by its parents, checked on every interpretation of a two-element domain
completeness: Herbrand gives ground instances, ground resolution refutes them, and the lifting lemma raises the proof
semi-decidability: a refutation is a proof and a stalled search is not an answer (Church)
equality is not built in, so a = a needs axioms or paramodulation
GATE CSE 2017 Set 1: I and IV follow from F: for all x exists y R(x,y), with two-element countermodels for II and III
GATE CSE 2020: for all x (p(x) -> W) is equivalent to exists x p(x) -> W, not to for all x p(x) -> W

the LR(1) item [A -> alpha . beta , a]: the lookahead is what may follow the whole right-hand side, not the symbol after the dot
closure with FIRST(beta a): six items in I0 of S -> C C where the LR(0) closure has three
the same kernel in state I2 gives three items, because there the second C is followed by the end marker alone
GOTO moves the dot over one symbol and closes again; the canonical collection of S -> C C has 10 states against 7
three pairs of canonical states share a core and differ only in lookahead: I3/I6, I4/I7, I8/I9
the reduce rule is local: [A -> alpha . , a] writes one action, in column a
the LR(1) reduce row is always a subset of the SLR row; of 27 completed items here exactly 1 is strict (R -> L in state 2 of the assignment grammar)
LALR merges states with equal cores and unions the lookaheads per item, not per state
the LALR state count equals the LR(0) count and the SLR count, always: 7/7, 13/13, 10/10, 12/12, 5/5, 4/4
merging cannot create a shift/reduce conflict, because the shift side is core-determined and the reduce side is not
merging can create a reduce/reduce conflict: the four-string grammar A -> c and B -> c end up on both d and e
the four-string grammar is LR(1) and not LALR(1): 14 canonical states, no conflict, 13 merged states, two reduce/reduce cells
resolving that conflict to the earlier production keeps 2 of the grammar's 4 strings; the canonical parser keeps 4
merging is not the only source of reduce/reduce: S -> A | B with A -> a and B -> a conflicts in LR(1) with 0 merges
the four rungs read one automaton; only canonical LR(1) can have more states than LR(0)
GATE CSE 2005: S -> ( S ) | a gives 6 SLR, 10 canonical and 6 LALR states, so n1 = n3 < n2
GATE CSE 2003: the SLR and LALR counts are necessarily equal, as a counting identity on cores
GATE CSE 2008: an LALR shift/reduce conflict exists exactly when the canonical LR(1) table has one

topics.subject: Compiler Design
topics.unit: Section 7: 'Lexical analysis, parsing, syntax-directed translation' — the recovery half of the word 'parsing', which no lesson owned
topics.topic: Error detection and recovery: the blank ACTION cell, panic mode, phrase-level repair and error productions
subtopics: error detection as a blank ACTION entry
the viable-prefix property and the correct-prefix guarantee
panic-mode recovery in LR parsers
panic-mode recovery in LL parsers
phrase-level recovery and its one-token repairs
error productions and the error token
the cost of each strategy, and what acceptance means afterwards
microtopics: an error is a missing ACTION[state, token] entry; the GOTO table has no terminal columns and cannot detect one
a canonical LR(1) parser stops at the same token as SLR but performs fewer reductions on the way: 218 against 344 on 777 erroneous strings
on id + ) id both stop at token 3 in state 7 with stack 0 3 7, after three reductions that were all licensed
on ( id SLR reduces three times before the error and canonical LR(1) reduces none
a viable prefix is a prefix of a right sentential form; 514 of them are enumerated up to length 9
the symbol string on the stack is always a viable prefix: 48 configurations on four valid parses, no exceptions
at every error the stack is viable and the stack plus the token is not: 777 of 777
no LR parser ever shifts a terminal the table rejected, which is why detection is at the earliest token
panic mode: scan down the stack for a state with a GOTO on A, pop above it, discard to a token that can follow A, push GOTO(s, A)
on id id that is 1 pop, 1 discard and a push of GOTO(0, E) = 3, then acceptance
on empty parentheses it is 0 pops and 0 discards, and the missing expression is supplied by the recovery
the rule as written loops when the offending token is already in FOLLOW of the chosen nonterminal
on id + ) id the configuration recurs six times before a report cap stops it
the progress guard: if the same stack and position recur, delete the token; one forced deletion ends the cycle
the guarded run reports four times and accepts id +, which is a repair and not the program that was written
popping past a state that covers a nonterminal deletes a phrase that had been parsed correctly
LL panic mode uses FOLLOW(A) as the synchronising set: token in FOLLOW(A) pops A, otherwise the token is discarded
on b b c one token is discarded; on b b b there are three reports, two discards and one pop
FOLLOW is context-free, so the sync set can accept a token that cannot occur at this point: the immediate error detection problem
phrase-level recovery enumerates 2n one-token repairs for n terminals: 1 deletion, n insertions and n-1 replacements
on id + ) id exactly one of the ten repairs parses to the end, and it is the deletion of the close bracket
the repair that reaches furthest is a replacement that still fails, so reach and acceptance are different tests
error productions add items wherever the nonterminal is expected: two productions take 12 states to 15
they add one conflict, a shift/reduce in state 7 on the close bracket, with no change to the language
the procedure is pop until error can be shifted, shift it, then delete offending tokens while in error mode
on id + ) id that is one report, two pops and two silent deletions; on ( id the error is at the end marker and deletion cannot repair it
acceptance after recovery means the repaired string parsed, never that the original was valid
GATE CSE 2015 Set 1: at a valid state the stack contains only a set of viable prefixes, answer (C)

canonical LR(1) items and the LALR merge

topics.unit: Section 7: 'Lexical analysis, parsing, syntax-directed translation' — the character level and the recovery half of lexical analysis
topics.topic: Lexical errors and lexer error handling: longest match, the two failures, panic mode and the progress guard
subtopics: what a token is, and the two decisions a lexer makes
longest match and the accepting state it remembers
the two ways a scan can fail
reported position against the position of the cause
the accepting-state fallback, and why a comment needs a commitment rule
classifying an error as lexical, syntactic or semantic
panic mode in a lexer, and the progress guard
syncing to a delimiter
counting tokens under a printed token specification
microtopics: a token is a class plus its lexeme; whitespace and comments are recognised and then skipped, so they are not tokens of the stream
the lexer makes exactly two decisions per position: where a token starts, and where it ends
longest match remembers the last accepting state passed and keeps going while a longer token is possible
a shortest-match lexer, which stops at the first accepting state, disagrees on 6 of the 13 corpus strings
the automaton has 24 states, 18 accepting, 638 character moves; a class may need several states (the literal needs four)
the automaton was cross-checked against an independently written matcher on all 2955 strings of length at most three and on all 13 corpus strings, with no disagreement
an empty string literal is one token; a hand-built automaton that omits the direct move from the opening quote to the closing quote reports a lexical error on a valid program
failure 1: no move from the start state (the dollar in x = 3 $ y; at character 7), so there is no partial token and no class to name
failure 2: a run that leaves the start state and reaches no accepting state (the unterminated literal)
the unterminated literal opens at character 5 and is reported at character 9: the reported position is where the run gave up, not where the cause is
a newline cannot appear inside a literal, which is why the failure lands at the end of the line rather than at the end of the file
the slash is accepting, so an unterminated comment raises no error under pure longest match: /, * and the word, three tokens
a real lexer commits to the comment on seeing the pair, which is a decision in the scanner driver and not in the transition table
the packed comment form gives 2 tokens and the spaced form 6, so the spaces change the program
keywords are not decided by the automaton: 5 keywords spelled out as paths would add 21 states, so the identifier is recognised first and its text looked up
ifx is one identifier and if is a keyword, because longest match decides the extent and the keyword table decides the class
lexical test: can this character be part of a token; syntactic test: may these tokens appear in this order; semantic test: do the types and names obey
a well-formed token in the wrong place is never a lexical error: on 3 + 4 ; every token is fine and the parser rejects token 1
12ab is not a lexical error in this language: it is number 12 then identifier ab, five tokens on x = 12ab;
panic mode in a lexer has no stack to pop; the only thing recovery can change is the position, so the counts are characters deleted and errors reported
x = 3 $ y; costs 1 deletion and gives x = 3 y ;; x = @@@ 3; costs 3 deletions in one pass and one message
the rule loops at an unterminated literal, because a newline can begin whitespace and so satisfies the rule: the deletion count is zero
the progress guard deletes the offending character when a pass deletes nothing, and the procedure terminates
the guarded repair leaves x = y = 2 ;, which the parser rejects: recovery preserves the scan, not the program
syncing to a semicolon skips 4 characters on x = @ y ; z = 1; and keeps the delimiter, so the token stream keeps its shape
GATE CSE 2026 Set 2: x1 23mm 78 y 7z zz5 14A 8H AaYcD is 9 words and 13 tokens, because an identifier begins with a letter
GATE CSE 2026 Set 1: S1 is the lexical error (an unclosed literal), S2 is fine (the semicolon is inside the quotes), S3 is the semantic error (char pointer to int pointer), answer C

topics.subject: Engineering Mathematics
topics.unit: Section 1: 'Probability and Statistics: Random variables' - the variance of a combination, which the clause does not name and no lesson owned
topics.topic: Variance of a sum, covariance, and the Chebyshev bound: three terms, one identity, two inequalities
subtopics: the variance as an average squared deviation, and the standard deviation
the joint distribution, its margins, and what the margins do not fix
covariance by the definition and by the shortcut
the correlation coefficient and its range
the three-term identity for the variance of a sum
uncorrelated against independent
the variance of a sum of n variables, and the count of terms
Markov's inequality and where it is attained
Chebyshev's inequality, the family that attains it, and how loose it is
turning a bound on a sample mean into a required sample size
microtopics: variance is the average squared deviation; the square is what stops the two sides cancelling
standard deviation is the square root, back in the data units
a variance of zero means a constant with probability one, not a small spread
a joint PMF puts a probability on every ordered pair; the margins are its row and column sums
margins do not rebuild the joint table: two tables can share both margins
covariance is the expected product of the two deviations; Cov(X,X) is Var(X)
the shortcut E[XY] - E[X]E[Y] equals the definition, checked to 12 decimal places on the same table
correlation is the covariance over the product of the standard deviations, so it is unit-free
rho lies in minus one to one; equality holds exactly when the two lie on a line with probability one
Var(X + Y) = Var X + Var Y + 2Cov, always, with no assumption
the variance of a sum can be read off the sum's own distribution by grouping atoms
drawing without replacement gives a negative covariance, so the sum varies less than independence suggests
the exact count is n sigma squared (N-n)/(N-1); drawing all N gives zero
with Y = X the sum has 4 Var(X), twice the naive answer
with Y = 1 - X the sum is constant, so two random parts can cancel exactly
for a difference the covariance is subtracted: Var(X-Y) = Var X + Var Y - 2Cov
zero covariance forbids a linear trend and nothing else: Y = X squared on a symmetric support is dependent
uncorrelated is enough for the variance identity, even when the pair is dependent
for n variables there are n variances and n(n-1)/2 unordered pairs; 6 terms for n = 3
independent identical copies give n sigma squared; the mean of n has sigma squared over n
perfectly correlated copies give n squared sigma squared, so averaging removes nothing
pairwise zero covariance is enough, and the exclusive-or triple shows pairwise independence without mutual independence
Markov: for X at least 0, P(X at least a) is at most E[X]/a, proved in one line from the mean
the two-point family attains Markov exactly, so no smaller bound holds for all non-negative variables
a Markov bound above 1 is vacuous, and Markov fails outright on a variable that can be negative
Chebyshev is Markov applied to the squared deviation: P(|X-mu| at least k sigma) is at most 1/k squared
the three-point family with mass 1/(2k squared) at plus and minus k has variance exactly 1 and attains the bound
k = 2 gives 1/4, k = 3 gives 1/9, k = 4 gives 1/16, and below k = 1 the bound exceeds 1
on a fair die the k = 2 bound is 0.25 while the truth is 0, and on ten coin flips the truth is 22/1024
the bound needs a finite variance, which a heavy tail may not have
a Chebyshev bound on the sample mean inverts to n at least sigma squared / (epsilon squared delta): 320 here
a normal quantile would ask for 62 on the same numbers, so the bound costs about five times as much
Var(aX+b) = a squared Var(X), while the standard deviation scales by the absolute value of a
GATE CSE 2021 Set 1 Q35: Cauchy-Schwarz kills the first statement and the sign kills the second; both false

topics.topic: File input and output in C: the stream, the six modes, the position, the return values and the two legality rules
subtopics: the FILE object as a handle to a stream, with a position, a buffer, an end flag and an error flag
the six mode strings and what each does to an existing file and to a missing one
fopen returns a null pointer on failure; using it is undefined behaviour
fgetc returns an int, and EOF is outside the byte range
fgets: at most n-1 characters, the newline kept, always terminated
return values as counts: fprintf characters, fscanf items, fread elements
the position: ftell, fseek with three origins, rewind
append writes at the end regardless of the position
update streams need a positioning call between directions
fclose flushes and reports failure with EOF
microtopics: a FILE pointer is a handle, not the file: the bytes are on the disk
the four fields every stdio call changes: position, buffer, end flag, error flag
stdin, stdout and stderr are open before main; printf is fprintf to stdout
a stream from fopen is fully buffered unless the file is an interactive device
mode r: existing file only, read from 0, size unchanged
mode w: truncates an existing file at the open, or creates it
mode a: creates if missing, keeps the content, writes at the end
mode r+ fails on a missing file, like r; the plus adds a direction, not existence
mode w+ empties the file and allows both directions
mode a+ creates if missing, reads from the start and writes at the end
b changes nothing on POSIX; on Windows it stops newline translation and 0x1A as end of file
a mode string outside the listed forms is undefined behaviour, not an error return
fopen returns a null pointer on failure and creates no stream
an empty file opens successfully and its first read returns EOF with the end flag set
perror reads errno; POSIX requires errno from a failing fopen and C alone does not
fgetc returns the byte as an int, and EOF is a negative constant outside 0..255
a 0xFF byte held in a signed char equals EOF, so the loop stops one byte in: 3 bytes against 1
whether plain char is signed is implementation-defined, which is why the answer is platform-specific
feof reports the last operation, so it is still 0 after the read of the last byte
while (!feof(fp)) runs one iteration too many and writes one byte of value 255
the read-and-test loop is the correct form and runs exactly once per byte
fgets stores at most n-1 characters, keeping the newline when it fits
fgets always terminates the buffer, and a short buffer splits a line rather than losing it
a failed fgets leaves the buffer untouched, so printing it repeats the previous line
gets was removed in C11 because it had no size argument
fprintf returns characters written; ten numbers with newlines are 21 bytes
fscanf returns items assigned; 12 34 x under three conversions gives 2 and leaves the position on x
fread and fwrite count elements, not bytes; four ints from ten bytes gives 2 and 2 bytes over
ftell is an offset from the start, and five single-byte reads give 5
fseek takes SEEK_SET, SEEK_CUR or SEEK_END; minus three from the end of eleven bytes is 8
a successful fseek clears the end flag; rewind also clears the error flag
only 0 or an ftell offset is portable for fseek on a text stream; any offset is defined on rb
seeking past the end and writing leaves a hole whose size the standard does not fix
in append modes the write goes to the end whatever the position is: abc becomes abcX
the same three statements in r+ overwrite the first byte: abc becomes Xbc
output then input on an update stream needs fflush, fseek, fsetpos or rewind
input then output needs fseek, fsetpos or rewind, unless the input met end of file
read-then-write on r+ with no positioning call is undefined, so there is no output to predict
fflush on an input stream is undefined in C and a no-op on POSIX
written bytes sit in the buffer until it fills, or until fflush or fclose
fclose flushes then releases, returning 0 or EOF
returning from main or calling exit flushes every stream; a crash does not
the five-step procedure: open, position, count, legality, close

topics.topic: Command-line arguments in C: argc, the argv pointer array, the null sentinel at argv[argc], and the conversion of a word into a number
subtopics: the shell splits the command line into words before the program starts
the program name is one of the words, so argc counts it
argv holds pointers to char, not characters; the strings are separate objects
argv[argc] is a null pointer by requirement of the standard
the sentinel may be compared and must not be read through
a counter loop bounded by argc with a strict inequality reads argc-1 slots
a loop bounded by argc inclusive fetches the null and is undefined if it uses it
with no parameters argc is 1 and argv[1] is the null pointer
the count test comes before any slot is read
atoi reads a prefix and cannot report failure, so abc and 0 both give 0
strtol writes an end pointer, and comparing it with the start is the error test
char *argv[] and char **argv are the same parameter
sizeof(argv) inside main is one pointer, not the array
the parameters and the strings are modifiable; writing past a string's terminator is not
where the strings live, and the text of argv[0], are implementation-defined
microtopics: the shell splits the line on blanks; the program never sees the original spacing
the first word is the program name, so three typed parameters give argc equal to four
argc minus one is the parameter count only after argc is known to be at least one
argv is an array of char pointers; the characters live in separate arrays
argv[0] is the name, so the first parameter is argv[1]
argv[2][0] is the first character of the second parameter; two subscripts, two dereferences
the array has argc+1 slots, and slot argc holds a null pointer
the standard says argv[argc] shall be a null pointer, as a constraint on main's parameters
comparing a null pointer is defined; printf with percent s on one is undefined
the sentinel exists so a loop can stop without the count
a counter loop starts at 1 and uses a strict bound of argc
atoi turns a non-numeric word into 0, so a loop starting at 0 can still print the right total
a bound of argc inclusive fetches the null at index argc and uses it, which is undefined
an empty run gives argc 1, never 0, and argv[1] holds the null pointer
atoi(argv[1]) on the empty run dereferences null, so the guard tests argc first
the standard requires only a nonnegative argc, so 0 is permitted and argv[0] is then not the name
argv[0][0] is the null character when no program name is available
atoi reads blanks, an optional sign and digits, then stops; 12abc gives 12
atoi cannot distinguish the word 0 from a word that is not a number
strtol writes the address where reading stopped, and end equals the start when nothing was converted
char *argv[] adjusts to char **argv in a parameter list
sizeof(argv) is the size of one pointer because the array type did not survive the parameter list
sizeof(*argv) is a pointer and sizeof(**argv) is one byte
the parameters and the strings are modifiable and keep their values until termination
modifiable is not roomy: writing past a string's own terminator is out of bounds
where the characters are stored, and the exact text of argv[0], are implementation-defined

topics.unit: Front end: the symbol table, shared by every phase (Section 7)
topics.topic: Symbol table organisation (linear list, search tree, hash table with chaining) and scope handling
subtopics: the symbol table as a dictionary of declarations: insert and lookup
the three classic organisations and what each one costs
the linear list: append plus a duplicate scan, quadratic to build
the search tree: cost is the height, which the insertion order decides
the hash table with separate chaining: buckets, collisions, chain length
occupation density and the load factor
scope as a stack of tables, pushed and popped
the lookup that walks outward and stops at the first match
the single table with duplicate keys and a log, as the alternative
where each entry goes: function name outward, parameters inward
microtopics: a symbol table is a map from a name to a record of attributes, not a table of run-time values
the record holds type, scope, storage class and offset; never the value
the two core operations are insert and lookup
the table is created during lexical analysis and read by every later phase
why 'not needed after parsing' is the false statement in a statement-selection item
linear list: append is free, the duplicate scan is the cost
linear list: comparisons per insert are 0 to n-1, totalling n(n-1)/2
eight names cost 28 comparisons, not 8 and not 36
re-inserting the last name scans all eight; an earlier name stops the scan at its position
search tree: cost is the height, and the insertion order decides the height
alphabetical insertion of eight names gives a chain of height 7 costing 28
median-first insertion gives height 3 costing 13
a plain search tree is never balanced by itself; AVL and red-black trees are what balance it
a tree of height 3 holds at most 15 nodes
hash table: hash the name, then search the chain in its bucket
char-code sum modulo 11 puts main and count in bucket 3
a collision is normal and chaining resolves it by appending
chain lengths must sum to the entry count: 1+2+2+1+1+1 = 8
six buckets used of eleven, longest chain 2
occupation density is entries over buckets: 8/11, and 25/152 = 0.16
inverting the density gives buckets per entry, which is a different quantity
with chaining the density may exceed 1; with open addressing it may not
one bucket restores the linear list and its worst case
expected O(1) needs a spreading hash function and a bounded load factor
every cost quoted is a claim about an assumption; name the case, average or worst
scope is a stack of tables, pushed on block entry and popped on exit
a lookup starts at the innermost table and stops at the first match
the first match is what makes shadowing work
a lookup costs O(d) for nesting depth d: constant per probe, linear in the probes
one entry per declaration, not one per spelling: five names, six declarations
six entries live but only five names reachable at the deepest point
the function's own name goes in the enclosing table; its parameters go in its own
putting the function name inward leaves callers unable to resolve it
why a prototype is needed: a later declaration is not in the table yet
the single table with duplicate keys and a log: O(1) lookup, amortised O(1) exit
the newest binding sits at the head of its chain, so the first match is the innermost
the trade-off between the two arrangements
the symbol table is compile-time; the activation record is run-time
the three question shapes and the five-step procedure

topics.unit: Section 1: 'Combinatorics: counting' at the junction with 'Graphs: connectivity'
topics.topic: Counting Eulerian circuits: the BEST theorem, arborescences and the de Bruijn graph
subtopics: the postman's question: how many closed walks use every arc once
Euler's two conditions for a digraph, and a graph that fails each
why the permutation count (m-1)! is not the answer
arborescences into a root: one exit per vertex, every path ending at the root
the BEST theorem and the meaning of each factor
the product alone, the tree count alone, and both together
the directed Matrix-Tree theorem: the Laplacian, the minor, the determinant
root independence of t_w on an Eulerian digraph
the de Bruijn graph and the sequences it counts
microtopics: a circuit is a cyclic object, so a rotation is the same circuit
the count is of walks, not of permutations of the arcs
the naive (m-1)! gives 120 on the complete digraph on three vertices where the truth is 3
balanced means in-degree equals out-degree at every vertex
balanced is necessary and not sufficient: three disjoint 2-cycles have no circuit
weak connectivity is the second condition, and strong connectivity is stronger than needed
an arborescence into w gives every vertex except w exactly one outgoing tree arc
every vertex must reach w, which is what excludes the cyclic exit choice
four exit choices minus the one 2-cycle leaves three trees on the three-vertex digraph
six exit choices minus the one 2-cycle leaves five trees on the doubled digraph
t_w is the same for every root of a connected Eulerian digraph
the directed Laplacian: in-degrees on the diagonal, minus the arc counts off it
a self-loop cancels on the diagonal, which is right because loops are never in a tree
delete the root row and column and the determinant is t_w
exact integer elimination, so the determinant is 5 and not 4.999999
the hub graph's minor is the identity, so its determinant is 1
the complete digraph on four vertices has 16 trees, which is n^(n-2)
the BEST theorem: ec = t_w times the product of (out-degree - 1) factorial
the tree names the exit kept back; the factorial orders the rest
the root contributes (out-degree - 1)! too, because fixing the first arc removes one rotation
0! is 1, so a leaf and a degree-2 vertex both contribute 1
a vertex of out-degree 3 is the first that contributes anything other than 1
the hub graph: t_w = 1, product 3! = 6, six circuits, and 4! would count each four times
the doubled digraph: t_w = 5, product 4, answer 20, confirmed by enumerating eight arcs
neither factor alone is the answer, which is why both appear as distractors
counting circuits that begin with a prescribed arc gives the same number
the de Bruijn graph B(2,3): four vertices, eight arcs, out-degree 2 everywhere
its t_w is 2 and its product is 1, so exactly two circuits
the two circuits decode to 00010111 and 00011101
all 256 eight-bit strings confirm the same two, after merging rotations
the de Bruijn count (k!)^(k^(n-1)) / k^n, checked for four pairs
counting Euler circuits in an undirected graph is a different and #P-complete problem
parallel arcs are distinguishable, and they raise the tree count
a positive tree count with zero circuits: the unbalanced counterexample
the four question shapes and the four-step procedure

the SMTP dialog: EHLO, MAIL FROM, RCPT TO, DATA, the message body, QUIT
SMTP reply codes and the four classes
the envelope against the header, and Bcc
FTP: control connection against data connection
FTP active and passive modes
MIME and base64 encoding, with the 76-character line
POP3 against IMAP

the greeting 220 is volunteered by the server, so it is not a client round trip
round trips = 6 + r, and connections stay at 1 whatever r is
fan-out to three domains: 9 + 3 x 7 = 30 round trips over 4 connections
pipelining (RFC 2920) turns the dialog into 4 round trips
one Received header per receiving server, newest at the top
the three buffers a MAIL command clears (RFC 5321 section 3.3)
354 is the only 3xx in base SMTP
dot-stuffing, and the five-character end of data
2xx success, 3xx intermediate, 4xx temporary, 5xx permanent, and the second digit as subject
five queued messages: one accepted, two retried, two bounced
552 full mailbox against 450 busy mailbox
six RCPT commands for three To, one Cc and two Bcc; four named addresses
MAIL FROM as the bounce address, recorded as Return-Path
a relay adds a trace field and must not change the envelope
FTP control on 21, data on 20 by default because RFC 959 uses L - 1
connections = 1 + n, round trips = 3 + 3n, and a listing is a transfer
login is paid once, not once per file
active: client sends PORT, server dials from 20; passive: client sends PASV, server answers 227, client dials
the control connection is stateful per session: directory, type, structure, mode, login
port 20 is a default, not what most implementations use (RFC 1579)
base64: 4 characters per 3 bytes, so the growth is a third and not a quarter

padding: 1 byte and 2 bytes both cost 4 characters
POP3 three states and delete-on-quit; IMAP server-side store and synchronised flags
100 messages of 20,000 bytes: 2,000,000 bytes by POP3 against 110,000 by IMAP
the IMAP saving is proportional to what is opened, not absolute
which of the four protocols is stateful, and for how long
8BITMIME removes the encoding cost when negotiated

prefix length, host bits and block size
splitting into 2^k equal subnets (fixed-length subnetting) and what it costs
usable host counts and the /31 and /32 exceptions
converting a host requirement into the smallest prefix that holds it
largest-first allocation and the alignment check
the free space decomposed into maximal aligned blocks
why the sum of hosts is not the sum of blocks
longest prefix match among the routes that match a destination
the lookup as a binary-trie walk
merging sibling prefixes into one aggregate
the hole: keeping a more specific route beside an aggregate
microtopics: a block starts at a multiple of its own size, so 100.64.0.48/26 names 100.64.0.0/26
size = 2^(32-p); alignment is the divisibility test, not a convention
network address = address AND mask(p); broadcast = network + size - 1
a split adds one prefix bit: 2^k equal subnets have prefix p+k and size 2^(32-p-k)
four /24s hold the same 1024 addresses as the /22 they came from, and two more reserved pairs
usable = 2^h - 2, with 254, 126, 62, 30, 14, 6, 2 as the sequence worth knowing
30 to 14 is not 15: the two reserved addresses are removed after the halving
/31 on a point-to-point link holds 2 hosts (RFC 3021 section 2.1), so 2^h - 2 gives a wrong 0
/32 is a host route: no network, no broadcast, and the formula would go negative
400 hosts needs a /23 because a /24 gives only 254 usable; 200 needs a /24 because a /25 gives 126
largest first, because a big block needs a big aligned hole and holes only shrink
the design of this lesson: 962 allocated of 1024, and 62 free in five blocks of 2, 4, 8, 16, 32
62 free addresses contain no /26, so a 40-host LAN does not fit while a 30-host LAN does
250 hosts fit a /24 but 288 addresses do not: the two effects are the reserved pair and rounding up
a failure by capacity is not a failure by fragmentation, and no order rescues it
longest prefix match maximises the prefix length among the matching routes, so a longer non-matching prefix is not a candidate
row order is irrelevant: reversed and rotated tables give the same seven answers
a destination inside the parent and outside every subnet is caught by the parent route
a binary trie walk is bounded by 32 steps for IPv4 and returns the deepest mark on the path
siblings are equal prefixes differing in the last prefix bit, and their parent is p-1
the longest common prefix of two non-siblings is shorter than p-1, so the only block covering both covers more
100.64.4.0/24 with 100.64.6.0/24 would aggregate to 100.64.4.0/22 and cover 512 unowned addresses
a hole stays as its own row: 100.64.0.0/22 plus 100.64.6.0/24 covers exactly 1280 addresses
