topics.topic: TCP's retransmission timeout and RTT estimation: the first-measurement rule, SRTT and RTTVAR in their fixed order, the one-second floor, Karn's rule and the backoff ladder
subtopics: the timer as one deadline for the oldest unacknowledged byte, restarted by an ACK of new data
the two costs of a badly chosen timer: spurious retransmission and a long wait after a real loss
the first measurement rule: SRTT = R, RTTVAR = R/2, RTO = 3R
the one-second floor on a computed timer, and why the rule keeps it
the update rule with alpha = 1/8 and beta = 1/4, and the order it must run in
the timer as centre plus four spreads, and what a spike does to each
Karn's rule: no sample from a retransmitted segment, and the timestamp exception
the doubling on each expiry, and the sixty-second ceiling
the closed form on a constant path, and the number of samples to convergence
the handshake rule that re-initialises a short timer to three seconds
microtopics: RTO is a duration the sender chooses; RTT is a duration it measures, so the two are never the same number
the timer guards the oldest unacknowledged byte, so it is not a countdown per segment
rules 5.1 to 5.3: start when data is sent and nothing is running, off when all is acknowledged, restart on an ACK of new data
with RTO 1200 ms a send at 0 and ACKs at 400 and 800 ms move the deadline to 1200, 1600 and 2000 ms
a 120 ms timer on a 400 ms path fires at 120, 240 and 360 ms: three copies, all before the first ACK
a 12000 ms timer on the same path waits 30 round trips for one loss
rule 2.1: the initial timer is 1 s; RFC 2988 used 3 s and a larger value is still permitted
rule 2.2: the first sample sets SRTT = R and RTTVAR = R/2, so one sample gives variance 0 but RTTVAR 200 for R = 400
rule 2.2 with G < 2R gives a computed timer of exactly 3R: 40 ms gives 120 ms
rule 2.4: a computed timer below 1 s is raised to 1 s, so 40 ms of RTT uses 1000 ms, a factor of 25
the floor clamps the timer only; SRTT and RTTVAR keep their computed values
rule 2.3 order: RTTVAR uses the OLD SRTT, stated explicitly in the document
the centre moves by one eighth of the gap: 400.2734 to 800 gives +49.9658 ms
the spread moves by one quarter of the gap: 91.4844 to 168.5449 ms on the same sample
swapping the two updates gives RTTVAR 156.0535 and RTO 1074.4531 instead of 168.5449 and 1124.4189
the swapped order always under-estimates the spread, so it always shortens the timer
the estimator is not the mean of the samples: 480 ms against 450.2393 ms on the five-sample trace
RTTVAR is a smoothed mean absolute deviation, not a variance, so 4 RTTVAR is not four standard deviations
the margin is max(G, 4 RTTVAR): with G = 1 ms it becomes 1 ms once the spread falls below 0.25 ms
a steady path multiplies the spread by three quarters per sample: RTTVAR(n) = (R/2)(0.75)^(n-1)
for R = 400 ms the computed timer is within ten per cent of R at sample 12, and 11.2627 ms of spread at sample 11 is not enough
one spike of 1600 ms after thirty steady samples gives SRTT 550, RTTVAR 300.0357 and RTO 1750.1429
the timer grows by a factor of 1.7501 from that one sample, and the excess decays by three quarters a sample
Karn's ambiguity: the ACK names a sequence number and both copies carry it, so the send time is unknown
scenario A: an ACK at 1250 after a copy at 1200 samples 50 ms for a 400 ms path, one eighth of the truth
scenario B: an ACK at 1600 timed from the original send samples 1600 ms for the same path, four times the truth
the timestamp option is the one documented exception, because it carries the send time
rule 5.5: RTO <- 2 RTO on each expiry, with no sample involved; the ACK still restarts the timer
the ladder from 1200 ms is 1200, 2400, 4800, 9600, 19200, 38400, 60000: six doublings to the cap
rule 2.5 permits a maximum only if it is at least 60 s, so a 10 s cap would be a violation
rule 5.7: a timer below 3 s is re-initialised to 3 s when data begins after a handshake
a timeout proves that no ACK arrived within RTO, not that the segment was lost
a timeout and three duplicate ACKs are different signals: only the first doubles the timer

topics.topic: TCP window scaling and the timestamps option: the 16-bit window field and its ceiling, the bandwidth-delay product, the shift count and its cap at 14, the two shift counters, PAWS and RTTM
subtopics: the sixteen-bit window field, the 65,535-byte ceiling and the throughput it allows at three round-trip times
the bandwidth-delay product, and why a window smaller than it leaves the link idle
the shift count: the true window as the field shifted left, and the ladder from 0 to 14
the derivation of the cap: twice the largest window below 2^31, so the window below 2^30
the handshake: the three-byte offer, both sides required, and the SYN field that is never scaled
the two shift counters, and the error factor 2^(difference of the counts)
choosing a shift from a receive buffer, and the two ways the choice fails at the ends of the range
the ten-byte timestamps option, its cost in the header, and its two jobs
PAWS: the modular comparison, the acknowledgement that must still be sent, and the 24-day invalidation
the echo that identifies which copy was acknowledged, and the rule that refuses an inflated sample
microtopics: the window field is 16 bits, so 65,535 bytes is the largest unscaled window
65,535 bytes per 100 ms is 5,242,800 bit/s; the same window gives 52,428,000 at 10 ms and 524,280 at 1 s
1 Gbit/s over 100 ms holds 12,500,000 bytes, so an unscaled window fills one part in 191 of the pipe
the option is kind 3, length 3, one shift-count byte, sent in the handshake only
the true window is SEG.WND << s, so the count is an exponent and not a multiplier
the top window is 2^30 - 2^14, which is 16,384 bytes short of a gibibyte
at count 14 and 100 ms the ceiling is 85,898,035,200 bit/s, exactly 2^14 times the unscaled figure
the old-or-new test reads a 32-bit space as a line by comparing with 2^31
twice the top window is 2,147,450,880, clearing 2^31 by 32,768; at count 15 it is 4,294,901,760 and fails
a received count above 14 is logged as an error and read as 14, which is safe because a sender may use less
scaling is enabled in a direction only if both handshake segments carried the option
the window field of a SYN or SYN,ACK is never scaled, so 65,535 read with count 7 is 128 times too large
a buffer of 8,000,000 needs count 7 because count 6 reaches only 4,194,240
a buffer of 1,000,000 needs count 4 because count 3 reaches only 524,280
both hosts then advertise 62,500, which means 8,000,000 one way and 1,000,000 the other
SEG.WND = RCV.WND >> Rcv.Wind.Shift and SND.WND = SEG.WND << Snd.Wind.Shift
the misreading factor is 2^(own count - peer count), here 2^3 = 8
the right shift is lossy: at count 7 the advertised field can lag the true window by up to 127 bytes
the scale applies to the window field only; the congestion window is a local 32-bit number
1,048,576 / 65,535 = 16.00024, so count 4 reaches 1,048,560 and is sixteen bytes short, and count 5 is needed
2^32 / 65,535 = 65,537, whose base-two logarithm is 16.00002, so the raw count is 17 and is clamped to 14
the timestamps option is kind 8, length 10: two one-byte fields and two four-byte fields
the header goes from 20 to 30 bytes with the timestamps option and to 34 with window scaling as well
payload efficiency with 1,460 bytes falls from 98.6486 to 97.9866 to 97.7242 per cent
TSecr is set to TS.Recent, which is updated only if SEG.TSval >= TS.Recent and SEG.SEQ <= Last.ACK.sent
an arrival is older when (saved - arriving) mod 2^32 lies strictly between 0 and 2^31
1,000 behind is rejected; 100 ahead gives 4,294,967,196 and is accepted
after the wrap, 100 against a saved 4,294,000,000 gives 4,293,999,900 and is accepted
a rejected segment still draws an acknowledgement, which is what detects a half-open connection
the clock ticks between 1 ms and 1 s, so the sign bit wraps in 24.855 days or 24,855 days
TS.Recent is invalidated after 24 days of idleness, which is below the worst-case wrap
the sequence space lasts 34.36 s at 1 Gbit/s, which is why a wrapped duplicate is possible at all
an echo of 1400 gives a 100 ms sample; an echo of 1000 gives 500 ms, the original rather than the copy
an echo may update the estimate only if the segment advances the left edge of the send window
a 40 ms path with a 60 ms pause reads 100 ms, 2.5 times the truth, and that echo is refused

topics.unit: Section 10: 'TCP- flow control and congestion control' - the option space the named clause rides in, and the shrinking window the flow-control field cannot avoid
topics.topic: TCP options and the forty-byte budget, with the MSS arithmetic and window retraction: the header ceiling, the option lengths and padding, MSS = MTU minus the fixed headers, options that cut the data and not the promise, the 2^s step, and the retraction bounded by 2^s - 1

the lengths of MSS, window scale, SACK-permitted, timestamps and MD5, and the rounding that turns 19 into 20
the MSS as the effective MTU minus only the fixed headers, data only, with 536 as the default
the rule that options reduce the data in the segment and never the advertised MSS

the three rules that make a shrinking window safe, and the bound of 2^s - 1 bytes

the data offset is 4 bits and counts 32-bit words, so it names 5 to 15 words
option lengths: MSS 4, window scale 3, SACK-permitted 2, timestamps 10, MD5 18
4 + 3 + 2 + 10 = 19, which rounds up to 20, giving a 40-byte header and 1440 bytes of data on a 1500-byte MTU
padding each option to its own word boundary gives 22 raw and 24 padded, so a 44-byte header and 1436 bytes of data
MSS counts data octets only: 576 gives 536, 1500 gives 1460, 9000 gives 8960, IPv6 1500 gives 1440, IPv6 1280 gives 1220, 68 gives 28
the MSS is the MTU minus only the fixed headers, so options are not subtracted from it
the sender must cut the data by the options it sends: 1460 data plus 40 bytes of options plus 20 of IP is 1520, twenty past the MTU
payload efficiency falls from 97.33 per cent with no options to 96.00 with 20 bytes, 95.73 with 24 and 94.67 with 40
536 is both the MSS of a 576-byte MTU and the default send MSS when no option arrives
65,535 in the MSS field means infinity for IPv6 jumbograms
the four handshake options plus MD5 cost 37, pad to 40, and fill the header to 60 bytes with 1420 bytes of data
one more four-byte option reaches 41 and cannot be sent in one header
a scaled window counts steps of 2^s, so the right edge is the acknowledgement plus a whole number of steps
at shift 7, acknowledgement 1000 can name 1128, 1256 or 1384, and the buffer end at 1300 is none of them
the appendix rows: 1256 (44 short), 1296 (4 short), 1301 (one past the buffer), 1173 (127 short)
the receiver honours any segment that would have been in window for any acknowledgement it sent
the first retransmission may ignore the window if it is out by less than 2^s; later ones obey the latest window
a scaled receiver tracks the largest right edge it has advertised
the retraction bound is 2^s - 1: zero at shift 0, 127 at shift 7, 1023 at shift 10, 16,383 at shift 14
16,383 bytes is 11.22 segments of 1460 bytes
stacks announce whole segments rounded up to the next step and suppress small window updates

1460 + 40 = 1500, which is 100 bytes over a 1400-byte path
1492 gives 1452, 1400 gives 1360, 1280 gives 1220 over IPv6 and 1240 over IPv4
the MSS subtracts only the fixed headers, so MSS plus headers equals the path MTU exactly
DF is what turns a silent drop into a measurement
the next-hop MTU counts the IP header, so 1400 means 1360 bytes of data
a zero in the field marks an unmodified router and forces a search
the plateau table's eleven values and the grouping that makes 1492 stand for 1536, 1500 and 1492
